claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by selective oxidation of Al and Ti.
Al and Ti preferentially diffuse outward from the FCC matrix at elevated temperatures.
Oxidizing exposure produces a dual-phase composite scale consisting primarily of Al2O3 with dispersed TiO2.
The Al2O3-TiO2 composite scale is coherent and protective.
The composite scale retards oxygen ingress, internal oxidation, and microstructural degradation.
Formation of the proposed protective scale preserves the alloy's strength and fatigue properties.
Lower oxygen activity in reducing environments destabilizes or prevents full development of the incipient protective scale.
Reducing exposure produces thinner, less adherent, or discontinuous oxides than oxidizing exposure.
Failure to form a continuous external scale under reducing conditions permits localized internal oxidation.
Internal oxidation and phase destabilization preferentially occur near additive-manufacturing grain boundaries or defects.
The starting additively manufactured alloy has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has a relatively homogeneous grain structure, although texture or porosity may remain from additive manufacturing.
The as-manufactured baseline has no thermally grown oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a continuous, relatively thick, adherent oxide scale with minimal subscale degradation relative to the baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner or patchy oxide layer together with voids, internal oxidation, or localized phase instability.
Oxide thickness, adherence, composition, and internal degradation can distinguish the proposed oxidation mechanisms under oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism applies from approximately 900 to 1100 °C over oxygen-rich through very-low-oxygen-activity atmospheres.
Conditions outside the stated temperature and oxygen-activity ranges may activate different degradation mechanisms.

contradictions.description: The oxidizing condition is variously defined as ambient air and as oxygen partial pressure near 1 atm. Ambient air has an oxygen partial pressure of roughly 0.21 atm, so these are materially different exposure conditions unless separate oxidizing cases are intended.
